scenario: An engineer says 'we could just build our own expense system.' Another says 'never build what we can buy.'
question: What is the sound starting principle?

options.text: Buy context capabilities that every company needs, and consider building core capabilities that differentiate you, while being honest about what is truly core.
Always build, because custom software fits perfectly.
Always buy, because engineering time is too precious for anything internal.

why: Both slogans are partly right and often wrong. An expense system rarely makes a company win, and teams love to call their own process unique when it is usually a common process with local habits.

scenario: The build estimate looks cheap and the vendor quote looks expensive. Someone wants to decide on the sticker prices.
question: How do you compare them honestly?

options.text: Estimate total cost of ownership over three to five years for each option: implementation, integration, migration, training, administration, maintenance, support and exit cost, with base, pessimistic and growth scenarios.
Compare the first-year license against the first-year development quote.
Choose the cheaper one and adjust the plan if costs grow.

why: Build cost is the down payment and upkeep is the mortgage. If one option is dramatically cheaper only under optimistic assumptions, treat that as a warning.

scenario: A process has outgrown its spreadsheet. The team debates building or buying but nobody has asked whether the process itself works.
question: Which option do people forget?

options.text: Improve or fix the manual process first. Software applied to a broken process automates the brokenness.
Buy software and let it define the process.
Build custom software that copies the current process exactly.

why: The real options are more than two: buy, buy and customize, low-code assembly, build custom, or improve the process. The fifth deserves respect.

scenario: A vendor demo went well and the team wants to sign.
question: What do you ask for before committing?

options.text: A trial or pilot with your own data and real workflows, evaluated by the people who will use it, plus reference customers you can speak to without the vendor present.
A discount for signing before the end of the quarter.
Nothing more. Demos are designed to show how it works.

why: Evidence from your own data beats vendor claims. Also ask how you get your data out, what limits apply and how pricing changes at renewal.

scenario: Operations staff are building dozens of apps on a low-code platform. They are fast and useful, but nobody can say who owns them.
question: What does the middle path need to stay healthy?

options.text: Governance: standards for ownership, naming, documentation, access and review, and awareness of platform limits for critical, high-volume systems.
Nothing. Speed is the whole point, and rules will slow it down.
Ban low-code tools and send all requests to engineering.

why: Without governance, low-code turns into sprawl, with undocumented apps owned by individuals. With it, the middle path often gives a better fit than packaged software and lower risk than custom builds.
